title: Six days and a rest (Genesis 1:6–2:3)
hookLine: the Church reads the days as a teaching about God and order, not a science textbook (CCC 337)

lines: THE SHAPE ENDS IN A DAY OFF.
cards: Were the six days of Genesis six real days, twenty-four hours each? People have argued about it at dinner tables for a long time. Some say yes.
Some say the days are ages. Some say science and the Bible are simply at war. The Catholic Church's answer steps around the fight.
The Catechism says scripture presents the work of creation symbolically, as a succession of six days of divine work, finished by the rest of the seventh. Not a stopwatch. A shape.
And the shape ends in something nobody expects from a creation story: a day off.

teach.b: Look at the shape. On the first three days, God separates: light from dark, the waters above from the waters below, the sea from the dry land. Rooms are built.

On the next three, God fills those rooms: sun, moon and stars for the light, birds and fish for the sky and sea, animals and finally human beings for the land. Separate, then fill. Form, then fullness.
Then the refrain. Over and over, God looks and sees that it is good.
At the end of the sixth day, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good."

The Catechism, at paragraph three thirty-seven, says the days teach the truth about creation: nothing exists that doesn't owe its existence to God, creation has its own order and goodness, and it is made for worship.

The Church holds that faith and science, rightly done, can't contradict each other, because the same God is behind both, and it leaves the science to scientists. Then the surprise. On the seventh day God makes nothing.
"He rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done."

teach.h: WHAT GOD MAKES HOLY: A DAY.
teach.b: God blesses that day and makes it holy.
Not a place, not a person: a day of rest. Catholics keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as their day of rest and worship, and the Catechism links it back to this seventh day.

how: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, attending Mass and, as the Church asks, setting aside work that keeps them from worship and rest; the Catechism ties this rest to the seventh day of Genesis.

o: to worship together on a feast
to bless and make something holy
to stop, to cease, to rest

games.q: what's inside the six days — tap the pairs.

s: the Catholic Church teaches the six days are a science textbook
the Catechism says creation is presented symbolically, as six days of divine work, to teach the truth about God and order.
in Genesis 2, what God blesses and makes holy is a day
the seventh day: God rests from all his work, then blesses it and makes it holy.
at the end of the sixth day, God calls creation good
very good: "and they were very good."

games.q: the heavens and the earth are finished, every room filled. it is the seventh day. what does God do?
o: God rests, and blesses the day and makes it holy.
games.why: "he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." the week ends in a blessed rest, not more work.

practice: Put the phone face down, out of reach, and let your shoulders drop; for these two minutes there's nothing to finish, fix, answer or plan. If your mind starts making a list, set it down like a tool on a bench.
In Genesis, rest isn't laziness, it's what comes after the work is very good, and if you pray, you can give thanks for one thing you made this week.

wordCard.voice: Shavat, the Hebrew verb behind Sabbath, to stop, to cease, to rest: what God does on the seventh day, and blesses. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: to stop, to cease, to rest. the verb in Genesis 2:2, and the root of Sabbath.

carryVoice: Your line: and he rested. The seventh day is the one God blesses. Day three hundred thirty-four, done.
